Configuration,Diameter — A flow-sensitive design combines DN700 pipelines with DN400 pipelines to achieve similar total pipeline investment costs.
Configuration,Diameter — A flow-sensitive design combines DN500 pipelines with DN400 pipelines to achieve similar total pipeline investment costs.
modeling — The integrated approach is used for modeling CO2 transport systems.
permeability map,predict — Trained CNN is used to predict the permeability map at the core scale in the workflow.
computational efficiency,prediction accuracy,process — The optimal sub-core volume size balances computational efficiency and prediction accuracy in the permeability upscaling process.
computational tool,process — The Darcy Flow Solver is used to determine the upscaled permeability at the core scale based on the predicted sub-core permeability map.
Integration — High-resolution CT images are integrated with broader-scale data to upscale permeability.
Permeability Determination — Small subvolumes were extracted from high-resolution CT images to determine permeability using LBM.
high-resolution,images — High-resolution CT images were obtained after processing the original micro-CT images.
algorithm,images — The high-resolution CT images were segmented using a threshold algorithm based on the grayscale histogram.
Integration — Low-resolution CT images are integrated with high-precision data to upscale permeability.
Permeability Prediction — Low-resolution CT images were used to train a CNN for permeability prediction at the core scale.

Prediction,capillary pressure,predict,relative permeability — 3D CNN is used to predict relative permeability and capillary pressure from 3D images of digital sandstones.<SEP>3D CNN is used to predict relative permeability and capillary pressure from 3D digital rock models.
Prediction — 3D digital rock models are used to predict 3D flow fields.
3D velocity field,permeability,predict — U-Net Architecture CNN is used to predict 3D velocity field and permeability from 3D digital rock models.
deep learning models,input — 3D Digital Rock Images are used as input for deep learning models to predict relative permeability and capillary pressure.
capillary pressure,predict,relative permeability — Physics-informed Machine Learning is used for predicting relative permeability and capillary pressure by combining with reinforcement learning.
determine,permeability values — LBM is used to determine permeability values of small subvolumes extracted from 3D Digital Rock Images.
Workflow Validation — The study sought to validate the effectiveness of Jiang et al. (2023)'s workflow for permeability upscaling modeling.
Model Evaluation — The study evaluated the required number of subvolumes needed to train the CNN to achieve acceptable prediction accuracy.
CT Image,Pore Network Model,Reconstruction — The Pore Network Model is reconstructed from high-resolution CT images.
Permeability Prediction — Predicted permeability map is extracted from the outer region of the large-scale rock sample using the trained CNN model.
Flow Flux Calculation — Flow flux within the whole core is calculated using the predicted permeability map by the Darcy flow solver.
images,processing — Micro-CT images were processed to enhance image quality and segment pore and solid phases.
extracted,low-resolution — Low-resolution subvolumes were extracted from the original coarse-scanned images.
Size,Subvolume — Case II subvolumes are of a specific size that highlights local heterogeneities in the rock.
Size,Subvolume — Case III subvolumes are of a specific size that highlights local heterogeneities in the rock.
Size,Subvolume — Case I subvolumes are of a specific size that highlights local heterogeneities in the rock.
Input,Workflow — The deep learning-based workflow used low-resolution CT images as input for permeability prediction.
Imaging,Rock Properties — CT images are used to visualize properties of crystalline formations.
Imaging,Rock Properties — CT images are used to visualize properties of metamorphic formations.
Imaging,Rock Properties — CT images are used to predict electrical conductivity of rocks.
Imaging,Rock Properties — CT images are used to predict seismic wave velocities of rocks.
Imaging,Rock Properties — CT images are used to predict mineralogical properties of rocks.
Imaging,Rock Properties — CT images are used to predict chemical properties of rocks.
Coordination Number Distribution — The pore network models are used to derive the coordination number distributions of subvolumes.
Calculation,Case I,Subvolume — Subvolumes are used for permeability calculations in Case I.
Calculation,Case II,Subvolume — Subvolumes are used for permeability calculations in Case II.
Calculation,Case III,Subvolume — Subvolumes are used for permeability calculations in Case III.
highest average,topologically stable,well-connected — Case III exhibits the highest average coordination number, indicating a well-connected and topologically stable network.
broad distribution,local heterogeneity,lower average — Case I shows a broader distribution of coordination number, suggesting more local heterogeneity and disconnected features.
Captured,Traditional — The Kozeny-Carman model traditionally captures the permeability-porosity relationship, but the machine learning-based approach effectively captured it more accurately.
Computational Domain,Solver — The Darcy flow solver was applied to the rectangular cuboid regions.
Computational Domain — Rectangular cuboid regions were extracted from the core sample for the Darcy flow solver.
network,representation — Pore geometries are extracted and used to construct the pore network model.
Computation,Upscaling — Darcy flow solvers are used to compute upscaled permeability from the predicted permeability distribution.

Boundary Conditions,Solver — Fixed pressure boundary conditions were imposed on the inlet and outlet sides of the Darcy flow solver.<SEP>Fixed pressure boundary conditions were applied to the Darcy flow solver.
Linear System,Solver — The Darcy flow solver solved the linear system constructed using the two-point flux approximation method.<SEP>The linear system was solved by the Darcy flow solver.
subvolume size — Case II and Case III are compared in terms of subvolume size.
subvolume size — Case I and Case III are compared in terms of subvolume size.
Agreement,Highest — Case III provided the highest prediction accuracy and closest agreement with experimental results among the tested cases.
subvolume size — Case II and Case I are compared in terms of subvolume size.
Darcy Flow Solver,calculate — Upscaled permeability of the entire core is calculated using a Darcy Flow Solver in the workflow.

circle.title: Saline Aquifers [geologicalbody] — Onshore saline aquifers are geological bodies containing saline water that can be used for CO2 storage. These aquifers provide significant storage capacity for CO2, both on a national and regional level, with Poland's storage portfolio including such aquifers. The saline aquifers in Poland have an estimated capacity of 3.8 gigatons and are located in the Baltic Basin. Onshore saline aquifers are r

Depleted Hydrocarbon Fields [geologicalbody] — Depleted hydrocarbon fields provide significant storage capacity for CO2.<SEP>Depleted hydrocarbon fields provide significant storage capacity for CO2 in Poland.<SEP>Geological formations that have been depleted of their hydrocarbon content and can be used for CO2 storage.<SEP>Fields with structural traps that provide storage potential for CO2.
Polands Geological Setting [geologicalbody] — The geological setting of Poland offers substantial sequestration opportunities across three major sedimentary regions.
Regulatory Framework [regulation] — Evolving regulatory frameworks in Poland are part of the assessment of CO2 storage potential.
Socio-Economic Factors [parameter] — Socio-economic factors are evaluated alongside geological and regulatory aspects in Poland.
European Union Climate Mandates [regulation] — Poland must meet the climate mandates set by the European Union.

Carbon Capture and Storage (CCS) [technology] — A technology for decarbonizing hard-to-abate sectors by capturing CO2 from industrial sources and storing it securely in geological formations.<SEP>A method for capturing and storing CO2 to reduce emissions and enhance oil recovery.<SEP>A portfolio of technologies for capturing carbon dioxide from sources and storing it in deep subsurface formations, including geological carbon storage (GCS).<SEP>

Geological CO2 Storage [process] — The process of storing CO2 in geological formations.<SEP>A method for storing CO2 in geological formations.<SEP>The process of storing CO2 in porous media for long-term geological purposes.
Storage Readiness Assessment [process] — An assessment of the readiness level for CO2 storage capacity in emerging CCS markets.
Technical Characterization [technology] — The process of characterizing the technical aspects of CCS projects.
Regulatory Clarity [technology] — The process of developing clear regulatory frameworks for CCS projects.<SEP>Regulatory frameworks to support the establishment of a CO2 storage network.
Infrastructure Development [technology] — The process of developing the necessary infrastructure for CCS projects.

Public Engagement [process] — The process of engaging the public in CCS projects.<SEP>A process involving the participation and communication with the public regarding the proposed CO2 storage project.<SEP>Strategies for engaging the public in the CCUS process
Transparent Governance [technology] — The process of ensuring transparent governance for CCS projects.<SEP>A governance approach that ensures clear and accountable decision-making in CCS projects.
Inclusive Community Participation [technology] — The process of involving the community inclusively in CCS projects.
Geological Formations [geologicalbody] — Rock units and structural features where CO2 is stored.<SEP>Various geological structures used for CO2 storage.
Historical Trends in CO2 Emissions [parameter] — Data showing the evolution of CO2 emissions by sector and fuel type in Poland over the past two decades.
Electricity Generation Sources [parameter] — Data showing the evolution of electricity generation sources in Poland over the past two decades.
Coal [material] — A fossil fuel that has historically contributed to CO2 emissions in Poland.

Oil [material] — Oil, a fossil fuel, has contributed to CO2 emissions in Poland. It is also known as petroleum and is a phase identified in the phase segmentation process. In the context of a study, oil is referred to as a chemical species present, represented by black in the greyscale renderings. Additionally, oil can be described as the remaining liquid in the pore space after reactive injection, and it is treat
Natural Gas [material] — A fossil fuel that has contributed to CO2 emissions in Poland.<SEP>A chemical species used for underground gas storage.
Electricity [geologicalbody] — The production of electricity is a major contributor to CO2 emissions in Poland.
Heat [geologicalbody] — The production of heat is a major contributor to CO2 emissions in Poland.
Transport [geologicalbody] — Transport is a contributor to CO2 emissions in Poland.<SEP>The process of transporting CO2 to storage sites.
Renewable Energy [material] — Renewable energy sources have increased to 21% of electricity generation in Poland by 2023.
Norwegian-Polish CCS Network Initiative [technology] — A collaborative project for carbon capture and storage.

Fault [geologicalbody] — A fault is a fracture or zone of fractures between two blocks of rock where some displacement has taken place. Faults are structural features in the Earth's crust that can affect the stability of injection wells, the integrity of wellbores, and CO2 storage. These fractures can act as barriers or pathways for fluids, facilitating the movement of CO2 and serving as pathways for CO2 flow from the tar

Reservoir [geologicalbody] — A reservoir is a rock unit that contains and/or can produce fluids, serving as a storage space for various types of fluids such as oil, gas, water, or CO2. Reservoirs are geological structures characterized by high porosity and permeability, making them suitable for CO2 storage and carbon sequestration efforts. Some reservoirs, particularly in the Rotliegend Group, can serve as storage areas for f
Pilot Studies [process] — Feasibility studies and practical demonstrations of CCS technologies.
Feasibility Assessments [process] — Evaluations of the practicality and economic viability of CCS projects.

EU CCS Directive [regulation] — A regulatory framework for carbon capture and storage in Europe.<SEP>The European Union directive that regulates carbon capture and storage (CCS).<SEP>A European Union directive related to carbon capture and storage.<SEP>European Union CCS Directive for carbon capture and storage.

CO2 Storage [process] — CO2 Storage involves the process of storing carbon dioxide (CO2) in geological formations, particularly deep saline aquifers, as part of CO2 sequestration projects. Advanced geological characterization techniques, simulation models, and risk assessment methodologies are utilized to evaluate various storage candidates. This process is highlighted as a key solution for CO2 storage in Poland, both in
ORLEN [technology] — A company involved in the CO2 storage assessment.

CO2 Leakage [risk] — CO2 Leakage refers to the escape of Carbon Dioxide (CO2) from storage reservoirs, particularly in the context of CO2 sequestration. This multifaceted risk involves various pathways, including mechanical instabilities such as fault reactivation and caprock fracturing, as well as material degradation due to carbonic acid formation from water impurities in CO2 streams. CO2 leakage can also occur thro

CO2 Plume [process] — CO2 plume refers to the movement and distribution of CO2 in storage areas and the subsurface after underground injection. This phenomenon is crucial for understanding the behavior of CO2 during storage operations and long-term assessments. CO2 plumes are regions of enhanced CO2 concentration in a reservoir or underground formation, characterized by their movement through the target aquifer and fau

Digital Twin [technology] — A digital twin is a comprehensive digital representation of a physical system or process, utilized for various purposes including simulation, optimization, and risk assessment. Specifically, it serves as a virtual representation of a physical asset, system, or process used for monitoring, modeling, and optimizing performance. Additionally, a digital twin is a method or model for creating a digital

Baltic Sea [geologicalbody] — A body of water within the Polish sector where potential CO2 storage sites are being assessed.<SEP>A body of water where restrictions exist for CO2 storage.<SEP>A body of water where offshore reservoirs are located in Poland.<SEP>A body of water in the northern part of the Atlantic Ocean, used for CO2 storage.
Sleipner Field [geologicalbody] — An offshore field where Equinor has pioneered CO2 storage.

Northern Lights Project [technology] — A large-scale CCS project led by Equinor, providing CO2 storage as a commercial service.<SEP>A project under the EU-funded ACCSESS program, which explores industrial CO2 transport from Polish facilities to North Sea storage locations.

Helsinki Convention [regulation] — A legal framework that may create complexities for CO2 storage in the Baltic Sea due to its prohibition on 'dumping'.<SEP>A regulation that requires consensus among all Baltic Sea states for activities that could affect marine environments.<SEP>A convention requiring unanimous Baltic Sea state approval for offshore development.
London Protocol [regulation] — A legal framework that contrasts with the Helsinki Convention, being more accommodating to CO2 storage initiatives.
Poland's ORLEN [technology] — A company aiming to capture, transport, and store 4 million metric tons of CO2 annually by 2035.
Equinor [technology] — A company contributing extensive CCS experience and leading several large-scale CCS projects.
Baltic Sea CCS Projects [technology] — Projects focused on carbon storage in the Baltic Sea, considering environmental, technical, and regulatory constraints.
Baltic Sea CCS [technology] — A type of carbon capture and storage (CCS) project focused on the Baltic Sea region.

MMV Systems [technology] — Measurement, monitoring, and verification systems dedicated to CO2 storage.<SEP>A monitoring approach that combines state-managed sensors with independent third-party audits to ensure cost-efficiency and regulatory compliance.
Onshore Saline Aquifers [geologicalbody] — Onshore geological formations containing underground water and used for CO2 storage.
Poland's Storage Potential [parameter] — The capacity of geological formations in Poland to store CO2.
Policy Evolution [parameter] — The changing regulatory landscape for CCS projects in Poland.
Regulatory Frameworks [regulation] — The set of rules and policies essential for the deployment of CCS projects.
Infrastructure Requirements [parameter] — The necessary infrastructure for CCS projects, including monitoring and verification systems.
Value Chain Integration Challenges [risk] — Challenges in integrating different stages of the CCS process.
Community Engagement [technology] — A method of involving local communities in the decision-making process of CCS projects.

CCUS [technology] — Carbon Capture, Utilisation and Storage (CCUS) technology refers to a set of technologies designed to reduce CO2 emissions by capturing carbon dioxide, utilizing it in various applications, and storing it in a safe and sustainable manner. CCUS encompasses a broader range of processes, including CO2 capture, utilization, and storage, making it a comprehensive solution aimed at addressing climate ch

Storage Readiness Levels [parameter] — A methodological framework for assessing storage capacity.<SEP>A set of levels indicating the readiness of a storage structure for CO2 injection.<SEP>A measure of the preparedness of different geological options for CO2 storage, indicating their suitability and readiness for deployment.
Resource-Reserve Pyramid [technology] — A methodological framework for assessing storage capacity.<SEP>A methodology for assessing geological sequestration potential.

EU CCS Directive 2009/31/EC [regulation] — A specific EU directive for safe geological CO2 storage.<SEP>A directive set by the European Union in 2009 to cover standards for safe geological CO2 storage, including site selection, monitoring, and liability.<SEP>A directive prompted Poland to transpose its provisions into national law by 2010 through amendments to the Geological and Mining Law.
2018 Directive 2018/2001 on Renewable Energy [regulation] — A specific EU directive on renewable energy.
2018 Directive 2018/2001 on renewable energy [regulation] — A directive supported synthetic fuels from captured CO2 in 2018.
EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) Directive [regulation] — A directive that exempted permanently stored CO2 from emission allowances under the EU ETS.

EU Innovation Fund [regulation] — A fund allocated €4.8B by 2024 for CCS/CCU projects.<SEP>A fund launched in 2018 that allocated €4.8B by 2024 for CCS/CCU projects.<SEP>A European funding mechanism that supports demonstration and pilot projects by improving the economic viability of marginal initiatives.
2011 CCS Act [regulation] — A national law that clarified exploration and storage licensing procedures and introduced environmental impact assessment requirements.

Polish Geological Institute [institution] — An institution responsible for geological surveys and estimates of CO2 storage capacity.<SEP>An institution providing estimates and guidance on MMV systems.<SEP>An institution providing estimates on MMV systems and their cost implications.

Geological and Mining Law [regulation] — A law that was amended to include provisions from the EU CCS Directive.<SEP>A legal document that defines the framework for onshore CO2 storage in Poland, particularly after the 2023 amendments.
Baltic Sea Basin [geologicalbody] — A basin estimated to have significant CO2 storage capacity in deep saline aquifers.

Deep Saline Aquifers [geologicalbody] — Aquifers in deep geological formations estimated to have significant CO2 storage capacity.<SEP>Primary reservoir types representing 90–93% of Poland’s total geological storage potential, positioned at depths ensuring supercritical CO2 conditions.<SEP>Reliable and feasible storage sites with abundant storage potential for CO2.
Net-Zero Industry Act [regulation] — An act related to achieving net-zero emissions in the industrial sector.<SEP>A legislative act aimed at achieving net-zero emissions in the industry sector.
Adopts EU Directive 2009/31/EC [regulation] — The act of adopting the European Union directive 2009/31/EC related to CCS.
Transposes EU Directive to Nat. Law [regulation] — The act of transposing the European Union directive into national law.
Introduces Nat. CCS Law [regulation] — The act of introducing a national law related to carbon capture and storage (CCS).
Cancels Bechatów CCS Project [regulation] — The act of canceling the Bechatów carbon capture and storage project.
Drafts PEP2040 with CCS [regulation] — The act of drafting the PEP2040 plan with carbon capture and storage (CCS) included.
Includes CCS in NECP Plan [regulation] — The act of including carbon capture and storage (CCS) in the National Energy and Climate Plan (NECP).
CCS aligns with EU Green Deal [regulation] — The act of aligning carbon capture and storage (CCS) with the European Union's Green Deal.
Revises PEP2040 for CCS [regulation] — The act of revising the PEP2040 plan for carbon capture and storage (CCS).
Aligns with EU CBAM [regulation] — The act of aligning with the European Union's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM).
Amends Geo & Mining Law [regulation] — The act of amending the geological and mining law to include carbon capture and storage (CCS).
Launches CCS Pilot Projects [regulation] — The act of launching pilot projects for carbon capture and storage (CCS).
Drafts CCUS Strategy [regulation] — The act of drafting a strategy for carbon capture, utilization, and storage (CCUS).
Funds EU-CCS Interconnector [regulation] — The act of funding the EU-CCS interconnector for carbon capture and storage (CCS) projects.
Allocates PLN 700B Energy Fund [regulation] — The act of allocating the PLN 700 billion energy fund for CCS projects.
CCS Directive 2009/31/EC [regulation] — A European Union directive for carbon capture and storage.
Green Deal [regulation] — A European Union initiative to make the EU's economy sustainable and climate-neutral by 2050.
CCS Act 2011 [regulation] — A national legislation in Poland related to carbon capture and storage.
NECP 2021–2030 [regulation] — The National Energy and Climate Plan for Poland.
PEP2040 [regulation] — The Polish Energy Policy until 2040.<SEP>A regulatory plan for Poland's CCS strategy from 2021 to 2040.

Clean Energy for EU Islands Initiative [regulation] — An initiative to support clean energy projects in EU islands.<SEP>A regulatory initiative aimed at developing clean energy hubs in the Baltic region.
Go4ECOPlanet Project [technology] — A funded project targeting 100% CO2 capture from the Kujawy cement plant, with liquefied CO2 transported to North Sea storage sites.
Kujawy Cement Plant [material] — A cement plant in Kujawy, Poland, responsible for 3.8% of the country's CO2 emissions.
Energy Transformation Fund [regulation] — A fund supporting onshore and offshore developments in CCUS projects.<SEP>A fund allocated to support CCUS infrastructure, research, and risk management.

Kujawy CCS Installation [technology] — A planned CCS installation in Kujawy, Poland, aimed at capturing 2.5 Mt CO2 annually by 2030.<SEP>A planned CCS installation in Poland aimed at capturing CO2 emissions.
EU ETS [regulation] — The European Union Emissions Trading System, a policy to reduce CO2 emissions.

Theoretical Capacity [process] — Represents the upper physical limit of CO2 storage, assuming all pore space within a geological formation is fully accessible for CO2 storage. Calculated using a volumetric approach.
Geological Formation [geologicalbody] — A rock unit where CO2 can be stored, encompassing formations, reservoirs, and saline aquifers.<SEP>The geological structure where CO2 is injected and stored.

Formation [geologicalbody] — Formation is a rock unit or structural feature that can store CO2, often featuring high porosity and permeability. It is characterized by depth and porosity-permeability, making it suitable for geological CO2 storage. In the context of hydrogeology and geomechanics, formations are rock units that can store and transport fluids. These formations are frequently used for storing CO2, both as rock uni
Formation Area [parameter] — The area of the geological formation (A) in square meters.
Gross Thickness [parameter] — The total thickness of the geological formation (h) in meters.

Porosity [parameter] — Porosity is a measurable quantity that describes the void space in rocks, influencing properties such as tensile strength, density of rock fractures, and the reservoir rock's ability to hold fluid. It is defined as the fraction of the volume of a rock sample that is filled with pore space, often denoted as ϕ, or the fraction of a rock's volume occupied by voids. Porosity measures the void spaces i
CO2 Density [parameter] — The density of CO2 at reservoir conditions (ρCO2) in kilograms per cubic meter.
Storage Efficiency Factor [parameter] — A factor (SCO2) reflecting the total pore accessibility in a geological formation.

Uncertainty [parameter] — The level of uncertainty in CO2 storage capacity estimates, reduced with more detailed site characterization.<SEP>The estimated plume uncertainty derived from 4D seismic data.<SEP>A measure of the variability or error in the predicted values of CO2 plume and seismic observation.<SEP>A measure of the variability or error in CO2 plume predictions due to unknown rock physics models.

Seal [geologicalbody] — A type of rock unit that can prevent the upward migration of stored CO2.<SEP>A layer of rock that acts as a barrier to prevent the upward movement of stored fluids, similar to the function of caprock.<SEP>A caprock over the reservoir that prevents the leakage of CO2.<SEP>A type of rock unit that can prevent fluids from moving through it.<SEP>A rock unit that serves as a barrier or cap.<SEP>A rock

Pore Volume [parameter] — The volume of space within rocks that can hold fluids, particularly relevant for CO2 storage.<SEP>Internal void space filled with loosely consolidated microcrystallites in halite aggregates.<SEP>A measurable quantity related to the volume of pores in geological structures.<SEP>The total volume of pores in the reservoir, used to explain the physical interpretation of the scaling factor χ.
Net-to-Gross Ratio [parameter] — The ratio of net thickness to gross thickness of rock units, used to calculate effective capacity.
Efficiency Factors [parameter] — Factors used to adjust theoretical capacity to effective capacity, accounting for irreducible water saturation and pressure limits.
Depth [parameter] — The vertical distance from the surface to the underground storage site, relevant for CO2 geological storage.

Salinity [parameter] — The concentration of salt in groundwater, which can affect the storage and movement of CO2.<SEP>A measurable quantity representing the concentration of dissolved salts in a fluid.

Storage Readiness Level (SRL) [parameter] — A standardized tool designed to assess the maturity of geological storage.<SEP>A standardized tool for assessing the maturity of geological sites for CO2 storage.<SEP>A measure of the preparedness for CO2 storage, used to rank storage sites.

Well [wellborecomponent] — A well is a borehole drilled into the ground to extract or inject fluids, such as CO2, and is a part of the wellbore component used for injection and production. Wells are also used in the simulation of injection and production processes, including both injectors and producers. The wellbore structure, which is used for drilling and installing components like the casing and cement sheath, serves as
Original Oil in Place (OOIP) [parameter] — The amount of oil originally present in the reservoir before any production.
Original Gas in Place (OGIP) [parameter] — The amount of gas originally present in the reservoir before any production.
Injection Costs [parameter] — Economic factor related to the cost of injecting CO2 into the reservoir.
Technical Constraints [parameter] — Operational limitations affecting CO2 storage.
Economic Constraints [parameter] — Financial limitations related to CO2 storage.
Regulatory Constraints [parameter] — Legal frameworks affecting CO2 storage.
Infrastructure Availability [parameter] — The presence and capability of existing facilities for CO2 storage.
Pilot Projects [parameter] — Limited operational data from test projects.
Legacy Well Integrity [parameter] — The condition of older wells that may affect CO2 storage.
Technology Readiness Level (TRL) System [technology] — A system that inspired the Storage Readiness Level (SRL) framework.
Storage Permit [regulation] — A document required for the storage of CO2, ensuring compliance with national and international regulations.
EIA [process] — An Environmental Impact Assessment, a process to evaluate the potential environmental effects of a proposed project.

Technical Appraisal [process] — A process involving detailed geological studies, including seismic surveys, well data analysis, and reservoir modeling, to estimate storage capacity and ensure containment integrity.
Permitting [process] — A process evaluating compliance with national and international regulations, which mandates environmental impact assessments and public engagement.

Operational Planning [process] — A process addressing logistical requirements, including transport infrastructure and monitoring systems for long-term site management.<SEP>A phase of operational planning that addresses logistical requirements, including transport infrastructure and monitoring systems for long-term site management.

Seismic Surveys [technology] — Geological studies involving the use of seismic waves to investigate the subsurface structure of a site.<SEP>Geophysical surveys used in 3D geological models for estimating static storage capacity.<SEP>Geophysical surveys that use seismic waves to image the subsurface.<SEP>Geophysical monitoring techniques that can predict CO2 plume saturation and delineate its boundaries.
Well Data Analysis [process] — Geological studies involving the analysis of data collected from wells to understand the subsurface structure of a site.

Reservoir Modeling [technology] — Geological studies involving the use of computer models to simulate the behavior of a reservoir and predict its performance.<SEP>Models used for simulating CO2 injection and plume migration in three dimensions to capture the full extent of CO2 behavior.
Storage Capacity [parameter] — The estimated volume of CO2 that can be stored in a given site, determined through geological studies.
Containment Integrity [risk] — The assurance that the CO2 will remain contained within the storage site, achieved through mechanisms such as structural trapping and residual trapping.

Transport Infrastructure [material] — Infrastructure required for the transportation of CO2 to and from the storage site.<SEP>Logistical requirements for long-term site management, including infrastructure for transporting CO2 to the storage site.

Monitoring Systems [technology] — Systems used for the long-term monitoring of the CO2 storage site to ensure operational compliance and safety.<SEP>Logistical requirements for long-term site management, including systems for monitoring the CO2 storage process.
SRL 2–3 [geologicalbody] — A specific classification for CO2 storage sites in Poland.
Prospect Unit [geologicalbody] — The most refined classification for CO2 storage sites, evaluated as commercially viable for development in CCS projects.

Reservoir Formation [geologicalbody] — A type of geological formation characterized by high porosity and permeability, essential for effective CO2 storage.<SEP>The rock unit structure where CO2 is injected and its plume behavior is observed, categorized as homogeneous, heterogeneous, or heterogeneous with geomechanics.

Storage Unit [geologicalbody] — A coherent, mappable subsurface body of reservoir rock located at sufficient depths, enabling secure CO2 containment with minimal leakage risk.<SEP>A larger geological body containing daughter units used for CO2 storage.

Daughter Unit [geologicalbody] — Specific structural and stratigraphic traps within a storage unit, leveraging established geological structures for safe CO2 storage.<SEP>A specific structural and stratigraphic trap contained within a storage unit used for CO2 storage.
Depleted Hydrocarbon Field [geologicalbody] — A type of daughter unit that has been depleted of hydrocarbons but can be used for CO2 storage.
3D Geological Model [technology] — A high-resolution model used for estimating static storage capacity, integrating well logs, core samples, seismic surveys, and other geophysical measurements.
Well Logs [material] — Geophysical data collected from boreholes, used in 3D geological models for estimating static storage capacity.

Core Samples [material] — Geological samples taken from boreholes, used in 3D geological models for estimating static storage capacity.<SEP>Physical samples of rock or soil taken from the subsurface for analysis.
Geophysical Measurements [technology] — A collection of geophysical techniques used in 3D geological models for estimating static storage capacity.

Seismic Inversion [process] — A technique for interpreting seismic data to estimate the properties of the subsurface.<SEP>Seismic data inversion to obtain saturation fields.<SEP>A process used to interpret CO2 plumes through seismic data.<SEP>The process of converting seismic data into an image of the subsurface.<SEP>A process that involves the use of measured seismic data to obtain parameters such as seismic velocities, acous

Permeability [parameter] — Permeability is a measurable quantity that describes the ability of a rock to allow fluid to pass through it. This property is crucial for understanding the flow of fluids through rock, which is essential for various applications, including reservoir analysis and geomechanical simulations. Permeability can be influenced by various factors such as calcite formation, slip along fault planes, and pla
Fluid Saturation [parameter] — A measurable quantity related to the amount of fluid in a given volume of rock.<SEP>The volume fraction of pore space occupied by a particular fluid phase.
Ceff [parameter] — The effective capacity of CO2 storage, calculated by adjusting the dynamic capacity with geological and operational risks.
Cdyn [parameter] — The dynamic capacity of CO2 storage, which is adjusted with risks in the risk-weighted approach.
Ri [parameter] — Risks associated with CO2 storage, such as fault reactivation, well leakage, and maximum allowable pressure.

Fault Reactivation [risk] — Fault reactivation refers to the phenomenon where faults in the reservoir are reactivated, leading to potential hazards, particularly during the process of gas storage. This risk is especially relevant in the context of CO2 storage, where reactivated faults can pose operational hazards. The reactivation of faults is particularly noted in Rotliegend reservoirs and UGS sites hosted by depleted hydro
Well Leakage [risk] — A risk associated with CO2 storage, where wells may leak leading to potential hazards.<SEP>A risk associated with leakage from wells.
Maximum Allowable Pressure [risk] — A risk associated with CO2 storage, where the pressure exceeds a maximum allowable limit leading to potential hazards.
Probabilistic and Monte Carlo-Type Methods [technology] — Techniques used to quantify risks in the risk-weighted approach to CO2 storage capacity.
Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis (MCDA) [technology] — A method to balance technical feasibility, economic viability, and environmental safety in the evaluation of CO2 storage potential.

Technical Feasibility [parameter] — A measure of the feasibility of CO2 storage from a technical perspective.<SEP>The ability of a technology or process to be successfully implemented under given conditions.<SEP>The feasibility of each site for investment.

Water-Saturated Porous Medium [geologicalbody] — A type of rock unit where CO2 can leak due to the absence of resistance.

Reservoir Pressure [parameter] — Reservoir Pressure refers to the measurable quantity of pressure within the subsurface reservoir. This pressure can change during CO2 injection and cessation, and is particularly important near critical levels, as it can lead to fault reactivation during CO2 storage operations. Reservoir pressure is also used for simulation purposes, often specified at the top of each reservoir complex. The pressu

Buoyancy Force [parameter] — A force that drives CO2 flow and is used to calculate the potential gradient of CO2.<SEP>The upward force exerted on a body immersed in a fluid due to the difference in density.

Injection Pressure [parameter] — Injection Pressure is a measurable quantity describing the pressure applied during the injection process.<SEP>The pressure applied to inject carbon dioxide (CO2) into geological formations.<SEP>A measurable quantity representing the pressure required to inject fluids into a reservoir.

Calcium [material] — Calcium, a material used in the description of layer development and the dissolution process.<SEP>An element that can be accelerated to form calcite in the process of sealing fractures.<SEP>A mineral present in the reservoir with a concentration of 0.993 mg/L.
Calcite Layer [geologicalbody] — A rock unit with a thickness proportional to the square root of time.

Well Cement Degradation and Wellbore Integrity in Geological CO2 Storages [process] — The process of degradation of well cement and its impact on wellbore integrity in geological CO2 storage projects.
Class G Cement [material] — A type of cement used in the study to which synthetic polypropylene fiber (PPF) was added to improve its properties.
Synthetic Polypropylene Fiber (PPF) [material] — A type of fiber added to Class G cement to improve its properties.

Cement Permeability [parameter] — A measurable quantity that refers to the ability of cement to allow fluid to pass through it.<SEP>A measurable quantity indicating the ability of cement to allow fluid to pass through.

Carbonation Depth [parameter] — A measurable quantity that refers to the depth to which carbonation occurs in cement.<SEP>A measurable quantity related to the depth of carbonation after the experiment.
Carbonation Rate [parameter] — A measurable quantity that refers to the rate at which carbonation occurs in cement.<SEP>A measurable quantity related to the rate of carbonation after the experiment.

Compressive Strength [parameter] — A measurable quantity that refers to the ability of cement to resist crushing.<SEP>A measurable quantity related to the compressive strength after the experiment.<SEP>The resistance of the formation to compressive forces.
Nano-Silica (Nano SiO2) [material] — A nanomaterial used as an additive to improve cement quality.
Nano-Alumina (Nano Al2O3) [material] — A nanomaterial used as an additive to improve cement quality.
Nano-Titanium Dioxide (Nano TiO2) [material] — A nanomaterial used as an additive to improve cement quality.
Carbon Nanotubes (CNTs) [material] — A nanomaterial used as an additive to improve cement quality.
Polymer/Clay Nanocomposites [material] — A nanomaterial used as an additive to improve cement quality.
Nanoglass Flakes (NGFS) [material] — A nanomaterial used as an additive to improve cement quality.

Basalt Powder [material] — A nanomaterial used as an additive in cement formulation.<SEP>A type of material used as an additive in cement formulation, characterized by low pozzolanic activity, a large inert fraction, and small particle size.
Geopolymer Cement [material] — A type of cement with a lower calcium oxide content, discovered to have better resistance with CO2-rich brine.

Porous Media [geologicalbody] — A rock formation with interconnected voids, through which fluids can flow.<SEP>The porous media relevant to CO2 geological storage.<SEP>A type of rock formation that allows fluids to pass through.
Well Integrity [parameter] — The ability of a well to maintain its structural integrity and prevent leakage of CO2.
Degradation [parameter] — The process of decline in the quality or state of cement over time in geological CO2 storage.

Stress [parameter] — The force per unit area exerted on a material, affecting the behavior of micro-annuli during geological CO2 storage.<SEP>A measurable quantity related to the mechanical conditions during geological CO2 storage.<SEP>A measurable quantity representing the internal forces per unit area within a material.<SEP>The internal force per unit area exerted by the medium on its boundaries.<SEP>The process of
Reactive Species [material] — Chemical species that can react with inhibitors in Portland cement.
Inhibitors [material] — Chemical substances added to Portland cement to reduce its reactivity.
Diffusion [process] — The carbonate concentration (C) changes over time due to the diffusion process through the cement layer.<SEP>The transport of solutes by random molecular motion.
Stress Field [UNKNOWN] — The change in stress field caused by CO2 injection may lead to a mechanical impact on the top seals.
Elastic Moduli [UNKNOWN] — Injecting CO2 decreases rock elastic moduli.
CO2 Flow [UNKNOWN] — Buoyancy force drives CO2 flow.
Casing/Cement [UNKNOWN] — The debonding interface between casing/cement or cement/formation is the primary cause for leakage of CO2.
Cement/Formation [UNKNOWN] — The debonding interface between casing/cement or cement/formation is the primary cause for leakage of CO2.

Reservoir Simulator [technology] — A software tool used for simulating multiphase flow in rock formations.<SEP>A well-constructed tool used in the study to evaluate the contribution of the geochemistry-heterogeneity-geomechanics trio to CO2 storage.<SEP>A computational tool used in the current study to analyze CO2 storage mechanisms in the Mae Moh Basin.
Mechanical Simulator [technology] — A software tool used for simulating mechanical behavior of rock formations.
Fault Slip [process] — The movement of a fault during CO2 injection.

Plastic Deformations [process] — The deformation of rock formations under pressure during CO2 injection.<SEP>Plastic deformations refer to the permanent deformation of the rock due to stress.<SEP>Deformations in the rock that are not recoverable.<SEP>A process involving the permanent deformation of the rock formation under applied stress.

Reservoir Integrity [risk] — The risk of losing the structural and functional integrity of the reservoir during CO2 injection.<SEP>The stability and safety of the reservoir.<SEP>The potential failure of the reservoir to contain stored CO2, leading to issues such as leakage and damage to the storage environment.

Flac3d [technology] — A computational tool used to calculate the mechanical state of the reservoir during CO2 injection.<SEP>A numerical modeling software used to evaluate the stress state and determine the stress difference.
Low-Carbon Fuels [material] — Fuels with a lower carbon footprint compared to traditional fuels.
Energy Efficiency [parameter] — A measure of how effectively energy is being used.
Depleted Oil/Gas Formations [geologicalbody] — Formations that have been exhausted of their oil or gas content.

Tectonic Fault [geologicalbody] — A tectonic fault is a geological feature characterized by a fracture in the Earth's crust, which may affect CO2 storage. It is a structural feature in the Earth's crust related to CO2 injection and can be described as active structural formations through which energy exchange occurs. Tectonic faults can cause elastic and plastic deformations, impacting permeability and porosity. These faults often

Plume [parameter] — A mass of fluid that moves through a porous medium.<SEP>The volume of CO2 spreading out in the reservoir.<SEP>A region in the subsurface where CO2 is stored, its size and location evolve over time.<SEP>A process representing the shape and behavior of CO2 in a plume, particularly in a polar domain.<SEP>A measurable quantity represented by a value of 1 where the plume is present (Sg exceeds a detect

Pressure Difference [parameter] — The difference in pressure between the injector and the far-field pore pressure.<SEP>Maps revealing the differences in pressure between different cases and along the core flow direction.
Pore Fluid [material] — The fluid found in the pores of rock formations.

Precipitation of Insoluble Salts [process] — A chemical process where insoluble salts precipitate due to interactions of carbonated water with minerals in the rock.<SEP>The process by which salts become insoluble in carbonated water.
Minerals [material] — Natural inorganic substances found in the rock formations.
CO2 Sequestration Technologies [technology] — Methods and models for the capture, transportation, and storage of CO2.
Dissolution of Carbon Dioxide in Brine [process] — A chemical process where carbon dioxide dissolves in brine.
Tectonic Faults [geologicalbody] — Tectonic faults that can be activated due to geomechanical effects.
Surface Infrastructure [risk] — Surface infrastructure that can be damaged due to deformation of the Earth surface above the storage area.

Seismic Activity [process] — Seismic activity in the neighboring regions due to the deformation of the Earth surface and tectonic fault activation.<SEP>Seismic events that can occur due to fault movement.<SEP>Seismic events associated with USS.

Fault Plane [geologicalbody] — The plane where the effective normal stress declines when the CO2 plume reaches the tectonic fault.<SEP>A structural feature within the geological formation, specifically the surface where shear stress and normal effective stress are evaluated.<SEP>The plane along which a fault has moved.
Fault Zone Permeability [parameter] — The permeability of the fault zone that can be enhanced by the slip of the fault.

Fault Core [geologicalbody] — The core of the tectonic fault where major cracks can form.<SEP>The central part of a fault where movement has occurred.<SEP>The central part of a fault zone, characterized by high deformation.<SEP>Fault Core is the central part of the fault where the maximum displacement occurs.<SEP>The central part of a fault structure that influences permeability.<SEP>The central part of a fault where mechanica

Target Reservoir [geologicalbody] — The underground formation where CO2 is injected and stored.<SEP>The reservoir being monitored, spanning lateral positions of 550-1,440 m and depths of 1,300-1,370 m.

Natural Fractures [geologicalbody] — Fractures formed by natural processes in the rock.<SEP>A system of fractures within the fault zone that can affect permeability.<SEP>Natural fractures are networks within the host rock that influence the permeability of the cells in the damage zone and the fault core.<SEP>Fractures found in the host rock.

Slip [parameter] — The act of a fault moving, causing displacement.<SEP>The movement or displacement along the fault system, which is accumulated during primary production and influences the stress redistribution during UGS and CGI.<SEP>Slip is mentioned as a parameter that changes during the process.
Mathematical Modeling [technology] — Methods used to simulate and predict the behavior of CO2 storage in geological formations.
Coupled Algorithms [technology] — Mathematical algorithms that solve the thermal, hydraulic, and mechanical processes simultaneously.
Sequentially Coupled Algorithms [technology] — Mathematical algorithms that solve the thermal, hydraulic, and mechanical processes sequentially.

Coupling Algorithm [technology] — A method used to exchange data between sequentially coupled algorithms.<SEP>An algorithm used to transfer coupling parameters between hydrodynamical and mechanical simulators at specific time instants.
TOUGH [technology] — Hydrodynamics simulator used for solving non-isothermal, multicomponent, multiphase flow subproblem.<SEP>A geomechanical simulator used in CO2 storage studies.
Coupled TOUGH-FLAC Simulations [technology] — Sequential approach applied to the solution of the hydrogeomechanical problem using TOUGH and FLAC3D simulators.
Sequential Coupled Approach [technology] — Less computationally expensive approach that allows flexibility in choosing the degree of coupling and coupling frequency.
Cap [geologicalbody] — Rock unit that serves as a seal for CO2 storage.
TOUGH-FLAC [technology] — A coupled simulator for TOUGH and FLAC used to investigate various problems related to CO2 storage.
FLAC [technology] — A geomechanical simulator used in CO2 storage studies.
PyLith [technology] — An open-source library used to couple TOUGH family codes with other geomechanical simulators.

CMG [technology] — A software package used for modeling of coupled thermal–hydraulic–mechanical processes in geological formations.<SEP>A commercial reservoir simulation tool used for predicting pressure and saturation maps in the reservoir.<SEP>A reservoir simulation model used for predicting pressure and saturation in the reservoir.<SEP>CMG is a computational model used for simulation.<SEP>Carbon Management System
CODE-BRIGHT [technology] — A software package used for modeling of coupled thermal–hydraulic–mechanical processes in geological formations.
MUFITS Academic Reservoir Simulator [technology] — A software package used for reservoir simulation.

FLAC3D Commercial Mechanical Simulator [technology] — A commercial software used for mechanical simulation.<SEP>A commercial software used for mechanical simulations, but not used in the current study.

Multiphase Flow [process] — The flow of multiple phases of fluids, such as carbon dioxide and pore fluids, in a geological formation.<SEP>A process that involves the simultaneous movement of multiple phases (fluids) in porous media.<SEP>The flow of multiple phases (CO2, brine, etc.) in porous media during the GCS process.<SEP>The physical process of fluid flow and transport in porous media during the GCS process.<SEP>Flow of
Permeability Evolution [process] — The change in permeability of rock formation in the tectonic fault zone during CO2 injection.

Bottomhole Pressure [parameter] — The pressure at the bottom of the wellbore during CO2 injection.<SEP>The pressure at the bottom of the well during CO2 injection.<SEP>The pressure measured at the bottom of the wellbore.<SEP>Pressure at the bottom of the well.<SEP>The pressure applied at the bottom of the well during the CO2 injection, which is 600 bar.<SEP>A measurable quantity used in simulations, with values of 350 bar (base) a
Formation Configuration [parameter] — The arrangement and properties of the rock formation in the geological structure.<SEP>The arrangement of the rock layers in the geological formation.
Stress Conditions [parameter] — The stress state in the geological formation during CO2 injection.<SEP>The stress state in the geological body during CO2 injection.
Water Vapor [material] — A component of the gas during CO2 injection.<SEP>A component in the gas phase during the injection process.

Mufits Reservoir Simulator [technology] — A software used for modeling Darcy flow caused by the injection of CO2, accounting for the dissolution of CO2 in brine, the presence of water vapor in the gas phase, brine salinity, temperature changes, convective heat transfer, and heat conduction.
NaCl [material] — A mineral used to characterize the brine salinity.<SEP>The sodium chloride component, denoted by subscript j=3.
Joule-Thomson Effect [process] — A phenomenon causing temperature changes in supercritical CO2.
Convective Heat Transfer [process] — A method of heat transfer involving the movement of fluids.
Heat Conduction [process] — A process of heat transfer through a material.
Aziz and Settari [technology] — A reference to a book (Aziz and Settari, 1979) that provides the governing equations for non-isothermal flow.
Pruess and Garcia [technology] — A reference to a book (Pruess and Garcia, 2002) that provides the governing equations for non-isothermal flow.
Pruess et al. [technology] — A reference to a book (Pruess et al., 2004) that provides the governing equations for non-isothermal flow.
Fanchi [technology] — A reference to a book (Fanchi, 2005) that provides the governing equations for non-isothermal flow.

Relative Permeability [parameter] — The relative permeability of the i-th phase, indicating the ability of a phase to flow through a porous medium relative to another phase.<SEP>The measurable quantity of relative permeability.<SEP>The relative permeability of high permeable sandstone and low perm clay/shale, based on Bennion and Bachu (2007).<SEP>Relative permeability predicted using 3D digital rock models.
Fluid Viscosity [parameter] — The viscosity of the fluid, a measure of its resistance to gradual deformation by shear stress.
Gravity Acceleration [parameter] — The acceleration due to gravity, denoted as g.

Specific Energy [parameter] — The specific energy of the saturated porous medium.<SEP>A measurable quantity representing the specific energy of the fluid, denoted as e.<SEP>The specific energy (e) is a component of the specific enthalpy (H) in the equation H = e + P/ρ, where P is the pressure and ρ is the density.
Enthalpy [parameter] — The enthalpy of the saturated porous medium.<SEP>A measurable quantity related to the internal energy of a system, including the energy associated with its temperature.
Heat Conductivity [parameter] — The heat conductivity of the saturated porous medium.
Gas-Water Capillary Pressure [parameter] — The capillary pressure between gas and water phases in the saturated porous medium.
Specific Heat Capacity of Rock [parameter] — The specific heat capacity of the rock phase.<SEP>The specific heat capacity of the reservoir rock, set to 0.81 kJ / (kg ⋅K).
Gas Phase [geologicalbody] — The parameters of the gas phase, denoted by subscript g.<SEP>A gaseous phase present in the system, often containing CO2.
Rock Phase [parameter] — The parameters of the rock phase, denoted by subscript r.
H2O [material] — The water component, denoted by subscript j=2.
Phase Densities [parameter] — A measurable quantity representing the density of fluid phases.
Viscosities [parameter] — A measurable quantity representing the fluid's resistance to flow.
Corey (1954) Curve [technology] — A method used for the relative permeability of gas in the storage reservoir.<SEP>A model for the relative permeability of gas

Van Genuchten (1980) Model [technology] — A model used for calculating the relative permeability of brine and capillary pressure in the storage reservoir.<SEP>A model for calculating the relative permeability of brine and capillary pressure
Flac3d Simulator [technology] — A simulator for computing the mechanical equilibrium state of the fluid-saturated formation

MUFITS [technology] — A hydrodynamics simulator used for solving the dynamic problem.<SEP>A reservoir simulator used in the study.<SEP>Hydrodynamical simulation tool<SEP>A simulator used in the numerical experiment for hydro-geomechanical modeling.<SEP>A modeling tool used for hydrodynamical simulations of CO2 injection.

Deformation [parameter] — A measurable quantity representing the change in shape of a material under stress.<SEP>The change in shape or size of the medium during the simulation.<SEP>The process of measuring the change in shape and size of a material under the influence of stress and temperature.<SEP>The elastic deformation in the mesh cells containing the fracture core.
Density Distribution [parameter] — A measurable quantity representing the variation in mass per unit volume throughout a material.
Linear Elastic Isotropic Model [technology] — A constitutive model implemented in FLAC3D based on Hooke’s law.
Elastoplastic Model [technology] — A constitutive model implemented in FLAC3D based on the Drucker-Prager yield condition.

Stress Tensor [parameter] — The stress tensor, 𝝈, is a measure of internal forces per unit area exerted by one part of a body on another. It includes the effective stress tensor, 𝝈′, which is defined as 𝝈 + 𝛼𝑃, where 𝑃 is the pore pressure and 𝛼 is the Biot coefficient.

Biot Coefficient [parameter] — The Biot coefficient, 𝛼, is a dimensionless quantity used in the study of fluid-saturated porous media to relate the pore pressure to the effective stress.<SEP>The coefficient related to the consolidation of the elastic porous medium.
Infinitesimal Strain Rate Tensor [parameter] — The infinitesimal strain rate tensor, 𝜺̇, is a measure of the rate of change of strain in a material, often used in continuum mechanics.
Infinitesimal Strain Tensor [parameter] — The infinitesimal strain tensor, 𝜺, is a measure of the deformation of a material, often used in continuum mechanics.
Displacement Distribution [parameter] — The displacement distribution, 𝐮, represents the change in position of particles in a material over time.

Velocity Distribution [parameter] — The velocity distribution, 𝐯, represents the rate of change of displacement of particles in a material over time.<SEP>The distribution of fluid velocity in the pore space, indicating the flow field.

Saturated Rock Density [parameter] — The saturated rock density, 𝜌, is the mass per unit volume of a rock when it is fully saturated with water.<SEP>The spatial distribution of saturated rock density in the rock.

Thermoelastic Model [technology] — A model in which stresses and deformations are linked with the temperature Ttotal distribution.<SEP>A model that links stresses and deformations with the temperature distribution, used to describe the behavior of the system under mechanical and thermal influences.
Temperature Ttotal [parameter] — The total temperature distribution in the thermoelastic model.

Velocity [parameter] — The rate of change of position of the medium.<SEP>The velocity (m s−1) of the fluid flow, obtained for each voxel of the image.<SEP>A measurable quantity representing the velocity of the fluid, denoted as v.
Temperature (Ttotal) [parameter] — The total temperature in the system, which is the sum of the actual temperature and pseudo-temperature.

MUFITS Reservoir Simulator [technology] — A reservoir simulator used for hydrodynamical simulations.<SEP>A reservoir simulator used for modeling the reservoir.<SEP>A reservoir simulator used for modeling the CO2 injection into a saline aquifer.

FLAC3D Mechanical Simulator [technology] — A mechanical simulator used for geomechanical simulations.<SEP>A mechanical simulator used for calculating plastic deformations due to changes in the stress state of the rock during CO2 injection.<SEP>A mechanical simulator used for studying the mechanical properties of the reservoir.<SEP>A mechanical simulator used for solving the mechanical equilibrium of the reservoir during CO2 injection.
Multiphase Darcy Non-Isothermal Flow [process] — The process of simulating multiphase Darcy non-isothermal flow in the reservoir.
Rock Density [parameter] — The density of the rock.<SEP>The density of the reservoir rock, represented by the variable 𝜌.
𝜙 [parameter] — Reservoir porosity field<SEP>𝜙 represents the rock porosity, a measurable quantity related to the fluid phase behavior.

𝜌𝑔 [material] — Gas phase density (CO2 with/without dissolved water vapor)

𝜌𝑟 [material] — Rock density
𝜙+ 𝜌𝑟(1 −𝜙) [process] — Calculation formula for liquid phase density

T(𝐫, 𝑡𝑖) [parameter] — Temperature field

MUFITS Simulator [technology] — A computational tool used for porosity and permeability estimation in the numerical simulation.<SEP>A simulator used for benchmark tests.<SEP>A simulator used for pure hydrodynamical modeling of CO2 injection.

Stress State [parameter] — The state of stress within the rock.<SEP>The current stress condition of the fault, evaluated by FLAC3D for determining the stress difference.<SEP>The current state of stress in the rock, which affects the mechanical properties and fluid flow.
Damage Rock Zone [geologicalbody] — The zone affected by inelastic deformations and where permeability modification occurs.
Carbon Dioxide Leakage [risk] — The risk of carbon dioxide escaping to the upper collectors through fault zones.

Fault Slip Line [geologicalbody] — A line along which a fault moves, indicating the direction of slip.<SEP>Fault Slip Line is a specific point or line along the fault where the movement of rock occurs.
Principal Fault Slip Line [geologicalbody] — A major slip line within a fault zone, affecting permeability.
Rock Layer [geologicalbody] — A layer of rock being deformed in the damage zone.
Fault Block Structure [geologicalbody] — The structure of Earth crust and sedimentation layer influencing the stress state of underground formation.
Rock Fractures [material] — Rock Fractures are fractures in the rock structure that affect the density and distribution of fractures as a function of distance to the fault slip line.
Damage Zone Envelope [geologicalbody] — A structural feature that confines the damage zone.

Rock Damage Zone [geologicalbody] — A rock structure that is related to the permeability of the fault.<SEP>A specific region in the vicinity of a tectonic fault where the rock permeability increases due to plastic deformations.
Localized Conduits [geologicalbody] — Faults with localized conduits for fluid flow.
Distributed Conduits [geologicalbody] — Faults with distributed conduits for fluid flow.
Combined Conduit-Barriers [geologicalbody] — Faults with a combination of conduits and barriers for fluid flow.
Localized Barriers [geologicalbody] — Faults with localized barriers for fluid flow.

Inelastic Deformations [process] — Irreversible deformations in tectonic faults due to rheological instability.<SEP>Inelastic deformations in the rock, which are represented by the symbol epsilon subscript p (ε𝑝).
Fracturing [process] — The process of rock fracturing under applied stress.

Dilatancy [process] — The irreversible increase in rock volume due to the increase in size of pores and fracture aperture.<SEP>An irreversible increase in rock volume due to the increase in size of pores and fracture aperture.<SEP>A measure of the mechanical properties of the reservoir rock, represented by dilatancy Λ.<SEP>A specific mechanical property of the storage aquifers and caprock.
Microfractures [geologicalbody] — Existing microfractures in rock samples that develop during deformation.<SEP>Small fractures in the rock.
Peak Stress [parameter] — The highest stress value before the initiation of microscopic fracture-like defects.

Mechanical Properties [parameter] — Properties of rock that can be altered by fractures, including effective mechanical properties and peak stress.<SEP>Attributes like bulk modulus (K), shear modulus (G), cohesion (c), and angle of internal friction (𝜃) that change towards the fault core.<SEP>Properties related to the mechanical behavior of the rock.<SEP>Mechanical properties of the storage aquifers and caprock, including bulk modul
Fractures [geologicalbody] — Structural features leading to the alteration of effective mechanical properties of rock.

Rock Sample [geologicalbody] — A sample used in laboratory conditions to measure the effects of triaxial stress loading.<SEP>A sample of rock used in the study, imaged at both high and low resolutions.<SEP>A sample of rock used in the study for permeability calculation.
Shear Stress Intensity [parameter] — The intensity of shear stress.
Rock Cohesion [material] — The measure of the strength of cohesion in rock.
Mean Stress [parameter] — The average stress value.

Shear Modulus [parameter] — The measure of a material's resistance to shear deformation.<SEP>The measure of the shear modulus of the elastic porous medium.<SEP>A specific mechanical property of the storage aquifers and caprock.

Dilatancy Coefficient [parameter] — A measure of the tendency of a rock to expand during deformation.<SEP>A measurable quantity that allows one to determine the increase in permeability of the rock damage zone.
Internal Friction Coefficient [parameter] — A measure of the resistance to deformation within a material.
Plastic Hardening Modulus [parameter] — A measure of the material's resistance to plastic deformation.
Fracture Porosity [parameter] — A measurable quantity that is the ratio of the volume of fractures to the total rock volume.
Fracture Intensity [parameter] — A measurable quantity determined experimentally as the ratio of total fracture length to the rock cross-section area.
Dilatancy Coefficient Equation [expression] — An equation expressing the relationship between dilatancy coefficient and the intensity of plastic shear deformations.
Rock Dilatancy Coefficient [parameter] — A coefficient related to the dilatancy of rocks, denoted by the Greek letter Lambda (Λ).
Plastic Shear Deformations [process] — Plastic shear deformations are the intensity of plastic shear deformations, represented by the second invariant of the shear plastic deformation.
Volume of Fractures Opened [parameter] — The volume of fractures opened due to rock dilatancy, represented as an increase in the rock volume due to inelastic deformations.
Fault Damage Zone [geologicalbody] — A damage zone near a fault, where the permeability is altered due to plastic deformations.
Flac3d Mechanical Simulator [technology] — A method used for mechanical simulations.
𝜀𝑝 [parameter] — Elastic volumetric deformation.
𝜀𝑣 [parameter] — Total volumetric deformation.
𝜀𝑒 [parameter] — Elastic deformations.
Δ𝜎′ [parameter] — Change in mean effective stress.

K [parameter] — Bulk modulus.<SEP>Permeability value of 20 GPa.<SEP>K is the total permeability of the cells in the damage zone and the fault core, calculated using the equation (54) and further refined in equation (55).
Shear Slip [process] — A type of shear deformation.

Main Crack [geologicalbody] — A larger fracture in the rock.<SEP>The main crack is a significant feature in the cells related to the fault core, which impacts the permeability in the vertical direction.<SEP>A significant fracture opening in the rock unit.

Shear Stress [parameter] — Applied shear stress.<SEP>The stress applied to the fracture that exceeds the friction force and resistant force.<SEP>The measurable quantity of shear stress on the fault plane, which reaches a critical value for fault activation.<SEP>The stress component that causes sliding along a fault, related to the friction coefficient and normal stress.<SEP>A measure of the force that tends to cause two adj
Friction Force [parameter] — Force due to friction.<SEP>The force resisting the motion of one surface sliding over another.
Natural Asperities [geologicalbody] — Natural features on the rock surface.
E [parameter] — A parameter related to fracture aperture.

Fracture Aperture [parameter] — The opening of a fracture due to slip, expressed as E_d = U_s * tg(d_m).<SEP>The hydraulic aperture of the main fracture, determined by the Barton and Choubey (1977) model.

Dilatancy Coefficient Λ [parameter] — A coefficient used to express the dynamic angle of dilatancy.<SEP>A measure of the change in volume of a rock sample under stress, which varies towards the fault core.
3D Geomechanical Modeling [technology] — A method used to evaluate mechanical and hydraulic fracture aperture based on rock stress state parameters and shear deformations.
Coupling Procedure [technology] — A procedure for the description of the activation of the fault core within the model.
Shear Stress (𝜏𝑛) [parameter] — The shear stress on the fault plane, calculated based on the normal effective stress and the inclination angle of the fault.
Normal Effective Stress (𝜎′𝑛) [parameter] — The normal effective stress on the fault plane, taking into account the plane strain conditions and the inclination angle of the fault.
Stress Difference (Δ𝜏) [parameter] — The difference in shear stress, calculated based on the stress state evaluated by FLAC3D.
Critical Value [parameter] — The threshold shear stress value, used to determine if the fault core should be activated.
α𝑢𝑝 [parameter] — A coefficient used in the equation to calculate the shear stress on the fault plane.
α𝑑𝑤 [parameter] — A coefficient used in the equation to calculate the stress difference based on the stress state.
𝑐 [parameter] — A constant term used in the equation to calculate the shear stress on the fault plane.
Lambda [parameter] — The dilatancy coefficient that varies between 0 and 1.
E_d [parameter] — The mechanical fracture aperture calculated using dilatancy and shear deformations.
Gamma [parameter] — The shear-strain increment, the square root of the second invariant of the strain increment deviator.
Delta_x [parameter] — The mesh cell length in direction perpendicular to the fault.
Pore Fluid Pressure [parameter] — The initial uniform pressure in the reservoir.<SEP>The pressure of the fluid within the pore space of a reservoir.
Viscosity [material] — The measure of the fluid's resistance to flow.<SEP>The measurable quantity of viscosity.<SEP>The fluid (brine) viscosity (Pa s).
G [parameter] — Modulus of rigidity value of 10 GPa.<SEP>A random matrix used in the FFT process.
Kf [parameter] — Fracture permeability value of 2 GPa.<SEP>A term used in the calculation of the saturated bulk modulus.
mu [parameter] — Viscosity value of 1 cP.
phi [parameter] — Porosity value of 0.1.
